passage:
NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage examines the role of fog as a water source in coastal forests.

Before sunrise, a forest ecologist checking collection trays beneath coastal trees found water pooled in trays that the previous evening had been dry. No rain had fallen. The moisture had arrived as fog, collecting on needles and leaves until droplets joined, fell, and struck the soil. The observation was not surprising by itself; anyone standing beneath a fog-wet tree may experience the same drip. The difficult question was whether this water merely dampened the surface or contributed meaningfully to the forest's supply.

Descriptions of forest water balance traditionally begin with rainfall. Rain gauges provide standardized measurements, streams reveal runoff, and wells track water stored underground. Fog is harder to measure. It moves horizontally, catches unevenly on vegetation, and may wet one ridge while leaving a nearby clearing nearly dry. A conventional rain gauge, designed to catch falling drops, can therefore report little precipitation during a night when tree crowns have intercepted substantial moisture.

The transfer begins when tiny airborne droplets collide with plant surfaces. Fine needles and leaves provide far more collecting area than bare ground. As droplets merge, some fall as fog drip. Some water remains on foliage and later evaporates, but another portion reaches the soil near roots. Leaves can also absorb limited moisture directly across their surfaces. These pathways suggest that fog may support plants both by adding water and by reducing how quickly leaves lose water to dry air.

To distinguish fog water from other sources, researchers combine measurements. Collectors placed in open areas and beneath tree crowns compare direct deposition with drip. Sensors record changes in soil moisture after foggy nights. In some regions, the ratios of stable forms of hydrogen and oxygen differ between fog, rain, and deeper groundwater. Those chemical signatures allow water sampled from stems to be compared with possible sources. A match does not mean that every molecule came from fog, but repeated patterns can reveal when plants draw on it.

Timing matters. In climates with wet winters and nearly rainless summers, frequent summer fog arrives when shallow soil is drying. A small input during that period may matter more than a larger winter input that falls when water is already abundant. Seedlings with short roots can be especially sensitive because they cannot reach deep reserves. Fog drip concentrated beneath mature trees may create moist patches where young plants survive longer than they would in exposed ground.

Yet the effect is not uniformly beneficial. A dense canopy captures fog efficiently but may keep much of the resulting drip close to established trees, where roots already compete strongly. Persistent leaf wetness can also favor some plant diseases. Wind direction, leaf shape, elevation, and the height of the fog layer alter collection from place to place. Researchers therefore resist converting one ridge's measurements into a fixed percentage for an entire coastline.

The most persuasive conclusion comes not from a wet tray, an isotope match, or a surviving seedling alone, but from the convergence of these observations. Physical collection establishes that fog reaches vegetation. Soil sensors show that some reaches the ground. Chemical evidence can connect that water to plant tissues, and seasonal studies reveal when the contribution is consequential. Together, the evidence changes fog from scenery into a measurable part of forest function.

The approach also explains why early studies sometimes seemed to disagree. A collector in a clearing measured atmospheric input, while a sensor beneath a crown measured water after the tree had concentrated it. Both observations could be accurate without representing the same stage of transfer. Identifying precisely what each instrument measures turns apparent contradiction into a description of the pathway.

This change also affects predictions. If warming shifts the height, frequency, or inland reach of coastal fog, rainfall totals alone may not describe the water stress forests experience. Models must account for a source that is locally uneven and technically difficult to measure. The fog's importance lies partly in that inconvenience: what standard instruments overlook may still shape where plants can persist.

paragraphs.function: Introduces an observation and the question it cannot answer alone.
Explains why standard rainfall measurement can omit fog.
Describes mechanisms by which fog affects plants.
Presents complementary measurement methods and a qualification.
Explains why a small seasonal input can be consequential.
Qualifies benefits and warns against broad generalization.
Extends the findings to climate modeling.

originality_notes: No origin-of-life theory, volcanic pool, ocean vent, ancient rock, or source anecdote is retained.
The evidence sequence concerns present-day forest hydrology.
